paragraphs: Removing parts of a neural network can produce a smaller model, but how well pruning works depends on how the original network was trained. This paper addresses the difficulty of predicting that dependence. It introduces a phenomenological model, grounded in statistical mechanics, that represents training influences through temperature-like and load-like parameters.

The central empirical observation is a sharp transition. Depending on the load-like parameter of the pruned network, increasing the temperature-like parameter before pruning can either help or hurt subsequent performance. The authors organize this behavior into three regimes based on the global structure of the pruned network’s loss landscape. Their explanation connects the opposing effects of temperature to transitions between those structures.

The framework matters because a training adjustment need not have the same pruning effect everywhere. The paper illustrates its use through three case studies: choosing which direction to adjust a hyperparameter, selecting a model to prune, and tuning Sharpness Aware Minimization for better pruning performance.
icml-2023-a-three-regime-model-of-networ.tldr: A three-regime model explains why the same kind of training adjustment can improve or impair subsequent network pruning.

paragraphs: Fitting training examples almost perfectly does not always prevent a neural network from predicting well on new data. This paper studies that possibility in overparameterized deep networks with ReLU activations. Under a well-separated data distribution and the lazy training regime, it proves that networks can reach Bayes-optimal classification error while achieving nearly zero training error.

The analysis connects overparameterization, benign overfitting, and the network’s Lipschitz constant, a measure related to how sharply its output can change. The results indicate that smoother functions that interpolate the training data generalize better. This gives a way to discuss the quality of an exact fit beyond simply asking whether the network has memorized its training examples.

For smooth ground-truth functions in the Neural Tangent Kernel regime, the authors show that generalization error approaches a constant order determined only by label noise and initialization noise. They also establish lower bounds concerning normalized margins and the smallest kernel eigenvalue. These are theoretical results within the stated distributional and training settings.
icml-2023-benign-overfitting-in-deep-neu.tldr: Under specified data and lazy-training conditions, overparameterized ReLU networks can nearly interpolate training data while achieving optimal classification error.

paragraphs: A language model can produce fluent text without reliably following every constraint a user supplies. InstructCTG addresses this gap by expressing constraints as natural-language instructions and training the model to generate sentences that satisfy them. The framework accommodates both linguistic constraints and constraints concerning other properties of the text.

The training data comes from existing natural text. Off-the-shelf language-processing tools and simple heuristics identify constraints that each sentence already satisfies. The method then turns those annotations into instructions, places them before the corresponding sentence, and fine-tunes a pretrained language model on the resulting pairs. This creates weak supervision from automatically annotated examples rather than requiring every instruction-and-answer pair to be written manually.

The approach makes constraint following part of what the model learns during fine-tuning. The abstract reports greater flexibility in supported constraint types than existing methods, without changing the decoding procedure. It also states that in-context learning lets the trained model adapt to new constraints without another round of training.
icml-2023-controlled-text-generation-wit.tldr: InstructCTG trains language models to follow text-generation constraints by converting automatically identified properties of sentences into natural-language instructions.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent lets many devices train collaboratively without a central server. This paper challenges the view that decentralization inevitably worsens generalization. It develops a theoretical connection between decentralized training and an average-direction version of Sharpness Aware Minimization, an approach concerned with the sensitivity of loss around the learned parameters.

The authors prove an asymptotic equivalence: decentralized SGD implicitly minimizes the loss associated with that average-direction method. Their result applies in general nonconvex settings without requiring beta-smoothness. The connection reveals a trade-off between optimization and regularization, providing a different way to interpret what decentralized updates do beyond distributing computation across devices.

The analysis identifies an implicit uncertainty-evaluation mechanism that can improve posterior estimation, a gradient-smoothing effect, and a sharpness-regularization effect that persists as total batch size grows. The last property supports a potential generalization advantage over centralized SGD in large-batch settings. The claim is about an asymptotic relationship and possible benefits, rather than a guarantee that every decentralized training run performs better.
icml-2023-decentralized-sgd-and-average-.tldr: An asymptotic connection to average-direction sharpness-aware minimization explains potential regularization and generalization benefits of decentralized SGD.

paragraphs: Continuous-time generative models can describe sequences through differential equations, but explicitly computing hidden-state recurrence can be expensive. Sharp changes in a sequence also create numerical difficulties during optimization. This paper introduces LS4, a generative model whose latent variables evolve through a state-space ordinary differential equation, to increase modeling capacity.

Its computational approach draws on deep state-space models known as S4. LS4 uses a convolutional representation that avoids explicitly evaluating the hidden-state recurrence. This representation matters because it provides a way to accelerate a continuous-time sequence model while retaining latent dynamics for describing the observed data.

On real-world datasets from the Monash Forecasting Repository, the authors report stronger marginal-distribution, classification, and prediction scores than previous continuous-time generative models. They also demonstrate modeling of highly stochastic sequences with sharp transitions. On irregularly sampled datasets, they report improved mean squared error and tighter variational lower bounds. The abstract additionally reports a hundredfold speed advantage over other baselines on long sequences, within the comparisons conducted.
icml-2023-deep-latent-state-space-models.tldr: LS4 uses a convolutional state-space formulation to generate complex time series more accurately and efficiently in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: An embodied agent searching for an object must connect what it sees with decisions about where to explore. Conventional object-navigation approaches often require extensive training in labeled visual environments and generalize poorly to unfamiliar objects and spaces. ESC instead transfers knowledge from pretrained models without navigation experience or additional training in those visual environments.

The method combines two sources of information. A vision-and-language model supplies prompt-based grounding for an open set of objects, while a commonsense language model reasons about rooms and objects. ESC expresses that commonsense information as soft logical predicates and uses them to guide exploration. This turns knowledge available in pretrained models into a basis for navigation actions.

Experiments on MP3D, HM3D, and RoboTHOR report substantial improvements over baselines and new state-of-the-art results for zero-shot object navigation. One example is a 288% relative success-rate improvement over CoW on MP3D. That figure describes a relative improvement in the reported comparison, supporting the usefulness of commonsense-guided exploration in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-esc-exploration-with-soft-comm.tldr: ESC turns pretrained visual and commonsense knowledge into exploration guidance for object navigation without navigation-specific training.

paragraphs: Accumulative poisoning attacks can build damage through a sequence of subtle manipulations followed by a trigger batch. In streaming data, poisoned examples may differ so little from clean ones that defenses based on those visible differences struggle to separate them. This paper investigates whether the model’s behavior can provide a more useful signal.

The authors introduce Memorization Discrepancy, an information measure that examines differences in model dynamics. Its purpose is to expose manipulation through changes in model outputs: examples that appear nearly indistinguishable at the data level can produce different learning dynamics. The method therefore uses information about how the model responds to samples to help discover poisoning.

Building on this measure, the paper proposes Discrepancy-aware Sample Correction as a defense against accumulative attacks. The authors study the measure’s properties and report extensive experiments characterizing it and verifying its effectiveness. The contribution is a model-level basis for detecting subtle poisoning and using that signal in a corrective defense, supported by the reported empirical investigation.
icml-2023-exploring-model-dynamics-for-a.tldr: Memorization Discrepancy uses differences in model dynamics to detect subtle accumulative poisoning and support a sample-correction defense.

paragraphs: This paper studies online node classification in a transductive setting, where prediction takes place on a given graph. Existing approaches can require a costly graph-kernel matrix inverse or many sampled spanning trees. Those demands make very large graphs difficult to handle, motivating an algorithm that can make predictions using more localized computation.

The authors first analyze an online relaxation approach and establish a regret guarantee when suitable parameterized graph kernels are chosen. They then develop FastONL, an approximate algorithm with its own regret guarantee. Its central component is a generalized local push method that approximates columns of an inverse matrix and works with several popular graph kernels.

FastONL’s per-prediction cost depends on a local graph volume and logarithmically on inverse approximation tolerance, while its memory requirement is linear. This connects scalability to the graph region involved in a prediction. Experiments report a better trade-off between local and global consistency, showing how the approximation can support both efficient computation and useful graph-wide prediction behavior.
icml-2023-fast-online-node-labeling-for-.tldr: FastONL approximates graph-kernel inverse columns locally to enable scalable online node labeling with theoretical regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks differ in which graph structures they can distinguish. Starting from relational pooling, this paper studies how to strengthen that distinguishing ability while connecting it to the Weisfeiler–Lehman hierarchy. Its initial mechanism assigns explicit node labels as additional features, giving message-passing networks more information for distinguishing graph structures.

The authors extend this idea to higher-dimensional Weisfeiler–Lehman methods through a two-parameter hierarchy called k,l-WL. They then incorporate subgraphs into a localized version of the framework. This broader organization encompasses many existing subgraph neural networks and allows the authors to compare expressivity as the two parameters change and relative to traditional k-WL.

The paper also discusses ways to reduce computational complexity when constructing practical neural-network instances. Its theoretical and experimental results support compatibility with any base graph neural network and the ability to improve expressivity. Reported performance gains on synthetic and real-world datasets complement the structural analysis, showing how a framework for distinguishing graphs can also support stronger predictive models.
icml-2023-from-relational-pooling-to-sub.tldr: A node-labeling and subgraph framework unifies graph-network expressivity enhancements through a generalized Weisfeiler–Lehman hierarchy.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in latent Markov decision processes with context available in hindsight. It asks how much regret a learner accumulates and how that cost depends on environmental variability and planning length. The authors develop a model-based framework that supports both model-optimistic and value-optimistic solvers.

Their regret bound depends on a variance quantity describing how deterministic the environment is, together with the numbers of contexts, states, actions, episodes, and the maximum transition degree. Crucially, planning horizon appears only through logarithmic factors. This yields a nearly horizon-free guarantee and a problem-dependent bound that reflects properties of the particular latent decision process.

The proof analyzes total variance for alpha vectors, which generalize value functions, using a truncation method. A complementary lower bound shows that the upper bound is minimax optimal, up to logarithmic factors, for variance-bounded problems when transition degree is constant. The result therefore identifies both an achievable learning guarantee and a matching difficulty scale under that stated restriction.
icml-2023-horizon-free-and-variance-depe.tldr: A model-based framework achieves variance-dependent regret with only logarithmic horizon dependence for latent decision processes with context in hindsight.

paragraphs: This paper studies robustness by examining a model along continuous paths between subpopulation distributions, such as distributions associated with different classes. The paths are Wasserstein geodesics: distribution-level interpolations that provide a structured way to move between populations. The aim is to assess and improve performance throughout that progression.

The method combines two operations. It augments training data using a worst-case Wasserstein barycenter along a connecting geodesic, and it regularizes the model so performance varies more smoothly along the path. These steps use the same distributional geometry to identify difficult interpolations and encourage more stable behavior across them.

The authors provide a theoretical robustness-improvement guarantee and investigate the contributions of interpolation location and sample size. Experiments on four datasets, including CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, support the approach. The abstract reports improvements of up to 7.7% in certifiable robustness on CIFAR-10 and 16.8% in empirical robustness on CIFAR-100. The strategy can also be combined with existing robust-training methods, making distributional interpolation an additional training tool.
icml-2023-interpolation-for-robust-learn.tldr: Training on difficult distributional interpolations and smoothing performance along Wasserstein geodesics improves robustness in the reported theory and experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets participants train locally, which also gives malicious participants opportunities to manipulate data or model updates. Server-side defenses can modify or reject suspicious updates. This paper finds that attacks with bursts in the number of malicious clients can circumvent existing defenses, motivating protection within the clients’ own training process.

LeadFL adds client self-defense alongside existing server defenses. Its core is a regularization term in local training designed to nullify the Hessian matrix of local gradients. The paper provides convergence analysis and a robustness guarantee expressed through a certified radius, connecting the proposed training change to formal properties of the method.

Empirical evaluations show mitigation of bursty attacks with both identically distributed and non-identically distributed client data. LeadFL frequently lowers backdoor accuracy from above 75% under state-of-the-art defenses to below 10%. Across the reported evaluations, its effect on main-task accuracy is smaller than that of the other client-side defenses. These results support combining protections at the server and client levels.
icml-2023-leadfl-client-self-defense-aga.tldr: LeadFL adds local-training regularization to server defenses to mitigate bursty backdoor and targeted attacks in federated learning.

paragraphs: A cluttered sequence of observations may combine several hidden entities, each following its own dynamics while interacting with the others. This paper develops a sequential-learning approach for that setting, including observations collected at irregular times. It represents the complex system through separate subsystems and an additional model of their changing interactions.

Each subsystem describes the continuous-time dynamics of a latent entity. A meta-system captures how those entities interact over time. The authors argue that this meta-system evolves within a simplex and is governed by projected differential equations. They also analyze projection operators through Bregman divergence and provide versions suitable for use with neural models.

The separation matters because entity behavior and interaction behavior are represented as distinct parts of the overall model. That structure gives the method a way to address clutter without treating all observed change as one undifferentiated process. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report advantages over state-of-the-art approaches when handling the complex, cluttered sequential data considered in the paper.
icml-2023-learning-to-decouple-complex-s.tldr: The method models cluttered sequences by separating latent-entity dynamics from a continuous-time meta-system describing their interactions.

paragraphs: Robust training usually addresses variations already represented or characterized in the training setting. This paper instead seeks robustness to unforeseen variations by drawing on out-of-distribution data. The central difficulty is that useful variation in an outside dataset comes bundled with a domain gap separating it from the target task.

The proposed algorithm has two stages. First, it trains an equivariant domain translator to map outside data toward the target distribution while preserving the variation being considered. Second, it regularizes the predictive model to produce consistent outputs on the translated data. Preserving variation during translation is central: the outside data must retain the property from which robustness is supposed to be learned.

The authors provide an analysis that bounds unforeseen robustness on the target distribution and motivates this procedure. Empirical results report improvements in both unforeseen and foreseen robustness over existing approaches. They also find that training the translator provides an effective criterion for selecting source data, linking the transfer mechanism to the choice of outside datasets.
icml-2023-learning-unforeseen-robustness.tldr: An equivariant domain translator transfers useful variations from outside data to improve robustness through output-consistency training.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders for sequences often use discrete-time mechanisms such as recurrent neural networks. Continuous-time alternatives are attractive for irregularly sampled observations, where the timing between measurements matters. Gaussian process variational autoencoders provide one such approach by placing a Gaussian process prior over latent variables, but their cubic computational cost limits scalability.

This paper introduces Markovian GPVAE, which exploits an equivalent discrete state-space representation of Markovian Gaussian processes. That representation makes Kalman filtering and smoothing available for training. The resulting computation scales linearly in time-series length, addressing the cost inherited from conventional Gaussian process calculations.

The key contribution is therefore a computational reformulation tied to the Markovian class of Gaussian process priors. It preserves the use of a Gaussian-process-based latent model while making training more scalable. Across several high-dimensional temporal and spatiotemporal tasks, the authors report favorable performance relative to existing approaches alongside strong computational scalability. These findings support the state-space representation as a practical route to this form of sequence modeling.
icml-2023-markovian-gaussian-process-var.tldr: Markovian GPVAE uses an equivalent state-space representation and Kalman methods to enable linear-time training of Gaussian-process sequence autoencoders.

paragraphs: Mixture proportion estimation asks how much of a mixed distribution comes from a particular component, using observations from both that component and the mixture. A central issue is identifiability: whether the available distributions determine the proportion. Earlier approaches use an irreducibility assumption to ensure that this estimation target can be identified.

This paper introduces a more general sufficient condition that covers several settings where irreducibility fails. The distinction matters because relaxing that assumption expands the situations in which estimation can be justified. The contribution does not remove the need for a condition; it establishes a broader one under which the problem can be addressed.

The authors also propose a resampling-based meta-algorithm. It adapts any existing mixture-proportion estimator designed for irreducibility to operate under the new condition, providing a way to reuse established methods. Empirical comparisons show improved estimation relative to baseline methods and a recently proposed regrouping approach. The paper thus combines a broader theoretical foundation with a reusable procedure for estimation.
icml-2023-mixture-proportion-estimation-.tldr: A broader sufficient condition and a resampling procedure extend mixture proportion estimation beyond the usual irreducibility assumption.

paragraphs: A watermark can help establish ownership of a neural network, but passive protection cannot fully prevent misuse. NNSplitter takes an active approach by dividing a model into an intentionally impaired version and a small collection of secrets needed to recover its original weights. Access to those secrets is restricted to authorized users through a trusted execution environment.

The impaired model contains obfuscated weights. The separate secrets record which weights were changed and their original values. This makes useful model operation depend on protected information beyond the distributed model itself. The approach therefore relies on controlled access to the secrets supported by the trusted execution environment.

The experiments demonstrate that changing very few weights can severely degrade performance. In the reported ResNet-18 example on CIFAR-10, modifying 275 of more than 11 million weights reduces accuracy to 10%. The abstract also reports stealthiness and resilience against norm clipping and fine-tuning attacks. These findings support the effectiveness of sparse weight obfuscation in the evaluated protection setting.
icml-2023-nnsplitter-an-active-defense-s.tldr: NNSplitter protects a neural network by obfuscating a small number of weights and restricting their original values to authorized users.

paragraphs: A graph neural network can expose information about private links between nodes. This paper studies graph reconstruction attacks, whose aim is to recover that adjacency structure. It examines several factors behind link leakage and uses a Markov-chain view of graph neural networks to investigate how reconstruction becomes possible.

The authors develop a flexible chain approximation and use information-theoretic reasoning to design both an attack and a defense. The attack adapts how it extracts private information from the trained model. The defense reduces link-sensitive information during training, aiming to make the resulting model less useful for reconstructing private connections.

These two mechanisms expose a tension between retaining information useful for reconstruction and limiting that information for privacy. The defense is reported to sharply reduce reconstruction fidelity with moderate loss in predictive accuracy. Experiments across six datasets and three common graph neural networks report state-of-the-art results. The findings connect a stronger attack analysis with a defense that explicitly addresses the information the attack exploits.
icml-2023-on-strengthening-and-defending.tldr: A Markov-chain approximation guides stronger graph reconstruction attacks and a defense that reduces link leakage with moderate accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Adversarial noise can disrupt a neural network even when the changes are subtle. This paper investigates that disruption through image phase, motivated by its relationship to human perception. The authors find that ordinarily trained models have insufficient robustness to perturbations at the phase level, identifying a particular weakness within image representations.

Their defense combines two mechanisms aimed at different components of the image. Phase-level adversarial training strengthens robustness to changes in phase patterns. An amplitude-based preprocessing operation mitigates perturbations in amplitude patterns. The design links the observed phase vulnerability to a training intervention while also addressing the other image component through preprocessing.

Experiments report substantial improvements in robust accuracy against multiple attacks, including adaptive attacks. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of the defense strategy. The contribution is both an investigation of where adversarial interference occurs and a joint response based on that investigation. Its reported success concerns the attacks evaluated, demonstrating the usefulness of considering phase and amplitude separately when building the defense.
icml-2023-phase-aware-adversarial-defens.tldr: Combining phase-level adversarial training with amplitude-based preprocessing improves robust accuracy against the evaluated attacks, including adaptive attacks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical account of learning from human comparisons and then using the learned reward to train a policy. It assumes that the underlying reward is linear. Under Bradley–Terry–Luce pairwise comparisons and Plackett–Luce comparisons among several alternatives, it proves convergence of maximum likelihood reward estimation in a particular semi-norm.

Accurate reward estimation in that sense does not automatically produce a good policy. The authors show that ordinary maximum likelihood estimation can fail at the policy-learning stage, while a pessimistic version gives good policy performance under a coverage assumption. This separates the statistical task of fitting preferences from the decision-making task that uses those fitted rewards.

For comparisons involving several alternatives, the paper also contrasts the full likelihood with a method that splits comparisons into pairs. Both converge under the Plackett–Luce model, but the full estimator is asymptotically more efficient. These results provide guidance for using comparison data and incorporating pessimism, with analysis that also applies to online RLHF and inverse reinforcement learning.
icml-2023-principled-reinforcement-learn.tldr: For linear rewards, comparison-based reward estimates can converge while policy learning still requires pessimism and sufficient coverage for good performance.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning guarantee can be more informative when it reflects how variable the environment actually is. Low-variance environments offer opportunities that a variance-independent regret bound cannot capture. This paper develops guarantees that adapt to those opportunities, including the deterministic setting, while retaining strong performance guarantees for stochastic environments.

The authors introduce two environment norms to describe fine-grained variance properties. They then design a model-based variant of the MVP algorithm and analyze regret in terms of those norms. The resulting bound is simultaneously minimax optimal for stochastic and deterministic Markov decision processes, establishing a single guarantee that matches the difficulty of both settings.

The paper also begins an investigation of variance-dependent guarantees for model-free methods. Its proposed algorithm uses a reference function with a capped-doubling update schedule. Complementary lower bounds help characterize the difficulty of the problems being studied. Together, these contributions make environmental variance central to the analysis and extend that perspective across both model-based and model-free reinforcement-learning approaches.
icml-2023-sharp-variance-dependent-bound.tldr: New variance measures support a model-based regret bound that is minimax optimal in both stochastic and deterministic environments.

paragraphs: Heterogeneous graphs contain different kinds of nodes, whose features can carry different meanings. This paper identifies a potential problem in ordinary message aggregation: transforming every neighbor into the receiving node’s feature space can entangle those meanings. SlotGAT addresses this issue by maintaining separate slots associated with different node types.

Messages pass through these slots so that representations remain in their own type-specific feature spaces. Within each message-passing layer, an attention mechanism aggregates information slot by slot. After the final layer, another attention mechanism learns how important the different slots are for the downstream task. This separates preserving distinct representations from deciding how much each should contribute.

The authors’ analysis indicates that the slots can preserve different semantics across feature spaces. They evaluate SlotGAT against 13 baselines on six datasets for node classification and link prediction, reporting superior performance. The findings support a design in which information from multiple node types remains distinguishable during propagation and is weighted according to the prediction task.
icml-2023-slotgat-slot-based-message-pas.tldr: SlotGAT preserves node-type semantics in separate message-passing slots and learns how to combine them for graph prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Learned vehicle-routing heuristics reduce reliance on manually designed rules, but often train and test on problems with the same size and node distribution. This paper studies a broader generalization setting in which both can change. The challenge is to prepare a learned solver for new routing tasks beyond its original training configuration.

The authors propose a generic meta-learning framework that trains a model initialization for rapid adaptation during inference. The desired outcome is a starting model that can adjust effectively to a new task. They also introduce a simple approximation method to reduce the overhead of training within this framework.

Experiments cover the traveling salesman problem and capacitated vehicle routing problem using both synthetic instances and benchmark instances. The reported results demonstrate the method’s effectiveness in the studied setting. Its contribution is to make adaptation across problem size and distribution an explicit training objective, connecting the way a solver is initialized to how it will be used when routing tasks change.
icml-2023-towards-omni-generalizable-neu.tldr: A meta-learning framework prepares neural routing solvers to adapt quickly across changes in problem size and node distribution.

paragraphs: A model’s ability to detect unfamiliar inputs can change during training, even when it trains only on in-distribution data. This paper observes across different settings that an intermediate training stage often detects out-of-distribution examples better than the final model. It identifies learning from atypical training samples as one critical contributor to that decline.

The proposed method, Unleashing Mask, aims to recover detection ability already present earlier in training. It uses a mask to identify memorized atypical samples, then either fine-tunes the model or prunes it using the mask to encourage forgetting them. The intervention works with in-distribution data and targets the model’s learned treatment of those samples.

Experiments and analysis support the method’s effectiveness. The finding shifts attention toward how ordinary training changes unfamiliar-input detection, alongside approaches that develop better scoring functions or use known outliers. The observed intermediate-stage advantage and the masking results suggest that retaining every memorized aspect of the training data can work against this particular detection objective.
icml-2023-unleashing-mask-explore-the-in.tldr: Unleashing Mask improves unfamiliar-input detection by identifying memorized atypical training samples and encouraging the model to forget them.

paragraphs: Pretraining on tabular data is difficult to share across datasets because tables can have different numbers and types of columns. Existing self-supervised methods often fail to use information across tables or generalize to new ones. XTab addresses this problem through a framework for pretraining tabular transformers on tables from multiple domains.

The framework uses independent featurizers to handle differences between tables and federated learning to pretrain a shared component. This arrangement gives table-specific inputs their own processing while allowing a common part of the model to learn across datasets. It provides a mechanism for transferring information despite mismatched table structures.

The authors evaluate XTab on 84 prediction tasks from the OpenML-AutoML Benchmark. They report consistent improvements in generalizability, learning speed, and performance across multiple tabular transformers. Pretraining FT-Transformer with XTab also produces superior performance to other state-of-the-art tabular deep-learning models on regression, binary classification, and multiclass classification tasks. These results support cross-table pretraining as a useful source of transferable learning.
icml-2023-xtab-cross-table-pretraining-f.tldr: XTab shares pretraining across structurally different tables to improve tabular transformers’ generalization, learning speed, and predictive performance.
